title: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable
oneLiner: The government's own review reached the conclusion industry had been making for years.
body: The review, led by Professor Graeme Samuel, found that assessment and approval under the Act duplicated state processes, took far longer than the statutory timeframes suggested, and gave proponents little certainty about what would be required of them.
contextBackground: The review was commissioned by a government sympathetic to industry and is nonetheless cited approvingly by environment groups, because it was equally damning about the Act's environmental record. It is the common reference point for everyone in the reform debate.
contextDisagreement: The finding itself is not disputed. What is disputed is which of the review's remedies to adopt: it recommended standards and an independent regulator, not deadlines.

evidenceItems.citation: Independent Review of the EPBC Act, final report, 2020 — chapter on efficiency and duplication

otherClaim.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040

claimItself.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040
claimItself.oneLiner: Legislation, licensing, site selection, workforce and construction each take years, and none has started.
claimItself.body: Starting from no regulator for power reactors, no licensed site and no construction supply chain, the sequence of repeal, regulatory design, licensing, approvals and a first-of-a-kind build is estimated by CSIRO and others at fifteen years or more. On that reckoning a decision taken now delivers first power around 2040 at the earliest.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Australia has no licensing regime, construction supply chain or operating workforce for nuclear power reactors

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The United Arab Emirates went from deciding to build nuclear power to first grid electricity in about twelve years, with no prior nuclear industry

claimItself.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
claimItself.oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
claimItself.body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.

otherClaim.title: The 2025 overhaul of national environment law will deliver faster approvals without weakening protection

claimItself.title: The 2025 overhaul of national environment law will deliver faster approvals without weakening protection
claimItself.oneLiner: The reforms have passed. Whether they do both of the things promised is the question as they roll out through 2026.
claimItself.body: The Environment Protection Reform Act passed on 28 November 2025 after a Labor–Greens deal, creating a National Environmental Protection Agency, national environmental standards, a streamlined assessment pathway and a ministerial national-interest exemption. Fossil fuel projects are excluded from the fast track and the exemption. The EPA began on 1 July 2026; the faster assessment provisions commence by 1 December 2026.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The reforms leave the minister, not the national environmental standards, as the final decision-maker for high-impact projects

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The streamlined pathway, bioregional plans and the national-interest exemption could let large-scale land clearing, critical-minerals mines and badly sited renewable projects through with less scrutiny than before

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Coal, gas and petroleum projects should be excluded from the streamlined approval pathway and the national-interest exemption
